The approach is based on a custom library that mirrors the Webots API, allowing the same controller code to be executed in the simulator and on the real TurtleBot3 with minimal modification. The library provides access to the robot motors, wheel encoders, inertial sensors and LiDAR, and is complemented by scripts that automate deployment and execution on the physical platform. It was used in a master-level course on introductory autonomous vehicles, and initial student feedback suggests that the approach reduces the perceived complexity of ROS-related infrastructure and helps learners focus on algorithmic logic and real-world behaviour.

title: Fault-Guided Cross-Layer Prediction for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection
summary: Feature reconstruction is widely used for unsupervised industrial anomaly detection in the single-class setting, where only normal images from one product category are available for training. We propose a single-class detector that asks what information one block can pass to another. We treat the depth of a frozen vision transformer as a sequence of discrete transitions. A directed predictor learns a block-to-block hidden-state transition pointwise over tokens. Adjacent-layer cosine similarity exposes four sharp fault lines in DINOv2 ViT-L, separating stable depth segments. The deepest blocks retain semantic context but lose local detail; a prediction from deep or shallow sources to sensitive targets therefore exposes the information that cannot be transported. The fault structure fixes the source and target roles, and the same rule transfers to ViT-B and RADIO-B. We use a bounded foreground prior calibrated solely on training images: it attenuates background evidence without also erasing defects outside the estimated foreground. Using one predictor architecture and a common training-only calibration protocol, image AUROC is 99.75 on MVTec-AD, 99.42 on VisA and 94.27 on Real-IAD. On Real-IAD the object-level AUROC is 96.26. At 256x256 pixel resolution, P-AUROC/P-AUPRO are 98.46/95.97 on MVTec-AD, 99.21/96.12 on VisA and 99.26/96.59 on Real-IAD.

title: H-TRIP: Exact Many-to-Many Distance Index for Multi-Robot Exploration
summary: Frontier-based exploration systems repeatedly evaluate geodesic travel costs between robot poses and candidate viewpoints, and tour-based planners consume the full pairwise distance matrix built from them. Recomputing these matrices with one graph search per source scales with the explored map size, whereas distance caches that refresh only locally affected or newly created frontiers can retain stale costs between surviving pairs when newly discovered free space creates a global shortcut. We present H-TRIP (Hierarchical Tropical Rank-one Incremental Propagation), an exact distance index grounded in Kleene algebra over the min-plus semiring for monotonically growing occupancy grids. H-TRIP partitions the known map into a spatial hierarchy with fixed boundary ports. Each unknown-to-free revelation is decomposed into efficient rank-one min-plus edge insertions at the affected leaf, and only decreased port-to-port summaries are propagated along its ancestor chain. A shared hierarchical lift evaluates the dense many-to-many matrix of shortest distances for all active query points on the occupancy map. We prove that sequential insertions preserve exact shortest-path distances on the grid. Benchmark experiments confirm exact agreement with reference searches on fully built maps and show that dense many-to-many queries at a few dozen viewpoints are up to two orders of magnitude faster than sequential k x BFS. On exploration runs with sixteen robots, in-loop queries on the growing occupancy graph are 2.21x-8.59x faster than co-scheduled k x BFS on maps with side 256, 512, and 1024 cells.

title: Describe Your Facial Expressions by Linking Image Encoders and Large Language Models
summary: This paper presents a novel task of describing human facial expressions of a facial image in natural language, which captures the nuances of facial actions and emotional states beyond traditional emotion categories or facial action units (AUs). To achieve the facial expression captioning model, we propose a three-stage training framework that trains a vision-to-language model using synthesized image-text pairs and the BLIP-2 pre-training techniques. To overcome the challenge of missing training image-text pairs for facial expression captioning, we propose a strategy that involves synthesizing and combining captions using GPT-3.5 and existing annotations on either emotion categories or AUs. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in generating captions that describe details of facial actions and emotions, as well as the inferential relationship between them, even when those emotions are not present in the training data. It is also demonstrated that the vision-to-language task enhances the performance of the intermediate visual features on both AU detection and emotion classification tasks.

title: How Far Can Untrained Neural Networks Go in Anomaly Detection? From Tables to Pixels
summary: Anomaly detection (AD) is often framed as a representation-learning problem, where strong performance is expected to require learned features or AD-specific optimization. However, this view can overlook the intrinsic separability of anomalies from normal references, even in the absence of learned representations. We therefore investigate how far untrained neural networks can go in anomaly detection. To this end, we propose PRISM, a framework combining fixed random nonlinear features with normal-reference Mahalanobis scoring for tabular detection and dense visual localization. Across 47 tabular datasets in ADBench, PRISM-T achieves the highest mean AUROC (86.4%) and the second-highest mean AUPRC (65.9%) among the compared methods. On MVTec AD and VisA, covering 27 visual categories, PRISM-V achieves mean image-level and pixel-level AUROCs of 90.4% and 96.4%, respectively. Notably, both models achieve these results without neural weight optimization or pretrained representations. A theoretical analysis further characterizes how nonlinear transformations affect the mean and covariance contributions to the Mahalanobis score gap, while empirical analyses examine the resulting score separability. These findings establish PRISM as both a competitive anomaly detector and a prior-to-learning baseline for assessing the added value of learned representations in anomaly detection.

title: TradingAgents: Multi-Agents LLM Financial Trading Framework
summary: A multi-agent framework using large language models for stock trading simulates real-world trading firms, improving performance metrics like cumulative returns and Sharpe ratio.

title: VibeVoice Technical Report
summary: VibeVoice synthesizes long-form multi-speaker speech using next-token diffusion and a highly efficient continuous speech tokenizer, achieving superior performance and fidelity.

title: Kronos: A Foundation Model for the Language of Financial Markets
summary: Kronos, a specialized pre-training framework for financial K-line data, outperforms existing models in forecasting and synthetic data generation through a unique tokenizer and autoregressive pre-training on a large dataset.

title: TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents
summary: TokenEconomizer reduces recurring token costs of coding agents across sequential real-world tasks by pruning irrelevant tools, injecting micro-skills, and interrupting failure loops.

title: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World
summary: Harness² improves agent execution harnesses through recursive task-level refinement and continual harness-level learning, boosting performance across benchmarks without ground-truth verifiers.

title: FreeToken: Efficient Edge-Native MoE Serving with Bandwidth-Adaptive Execution
summary: FreeToken is an edge-native Mixture-of-Experts serving system that dynamically maps computation and model state onto heterogeneous local hardware to run large open-weight models on personal machines.

title: Persistent Recursive Worlds Enable Autonomous Software Evolution
summary: Genesis organizes long-horizon software development around a persistent project rather than persistent agents, enabling multi-day compiler construction and numerical module reimplementation with low cost and high performance.

title: Unlimited OCR Works
summary: Unlimited OCR introduces Reference Sliding Window Attention to eliminate growing memory consumption during long-sequence OCR tasks, enabling efficient transcription of multiple pages in a single forward pass.

title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
summary: PagedAttention algorithm and vLLM system enhance the throughput of large language models by efficiently managing memory and reducing waste in the key-value cache.

title: OpenDevin: An Open Platform for AI Software Developers as Generalist Agents
summary: OpenDevin is a platform for developing AI agents that interact with the world by writing code, using command lines, and browsing the web, with support for multiple agents and evaluation benchmarks.

title: Very Large-Scale Multi-Agent Simulation in AgentScope
summary: Enhancements to the AgentScope platform improve scalability, efficiency, and ease of use for large-scale multi-agent simulations through distributed mechanisms, flexible environments, and user-friendly tools.

title: AgentScope 1.0: A Developer-Centric Framework for Building Agentic Applications
summary: AgentScope enhances agentic applications by providing flexible tool-based interactions, unified interfaces, and advanced infrastructure based on the ReAct paradigm, supporting efficient and safe development and deployment.

title: HairDeck: Animation-Ready Stylized Hair Cards from a Single Image
summary: HairDeck generates stylized hair cards and spring-bone animations as unordered token sets using a diffusion transformer, improving accuracy and speed over prior methods.

title: Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory
summary: Mem0, a memory-centric architecture with graph-based memory, enhances long-term conversational coherence in LLMs by efficiently extracting, consolidating, and retrieving information, outperforming existing memory systems in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.

title: Democratizing Robot-Use Agents: A Unified Harness with Open Models
summary: Uni-robot-agent enables open-weight robot-use agents to surpass proprietary models in zero-shot manipulation and suggests joint development of four core capabilities for future training.

title: VisSearch-Bench: Evaluating Long Horizon Visual Search in Multimodal Agents
summary: VisSearch-Bench evaluates multimodal agents on visually intensive search tasks that require integrating visual context with external information, showing that even the best system fully solves only 26.47% of tasks.

title: ARIS: Autonomous Research via Adversarial Multi-Agent Collaboration
summary: ARIS is an open-source research harness that uses cross-model adversarial collaboration to ensure reliable long-term research outcomes through coordinated execution, orchestration, and assurance layers.

title: WeVisOne-VL: Unified Visual Perception from Objects to Pixels
summary: WeVisOne-VL unifies object-level and pixel-level visual perception via structured token prediction, supporting detection, localization, counting, OCR, segmentation, and matting with a lightweight pixel decoder and multi-stage training.

title: The Other Half of the Memory Wall: Serving 35B MoEs from SSD with Trained Routing Prediction
summary: Edge0 enables efficient mixture-of-experts inference on consumer hardware by predicting expert routing ahead of time and using recovery adapters to maintain quality with minimal active memory.

title: MinerU2.5: A Decoupled Vision-Language Model for Efficient High-Resolution Document Parsing
summary: MinerU2.5, a 1.2B-parameter document parsing vision-language model, achieves state-of-the-art recognition accuracy with computational efficiency through a coarse-to-fine parsing strategy.

title: SmolDocling: An ultra-compact vision-language model for end-to-end multi-modal document conversion
summary: SmolDocling is a compact vision-language model that performs end-to-end document conversion with robust performance across various document types using 256M parameters and a new markup format.

title: PaddleOCR-VL-1.6: Expanding the Frontier of Document Parsing with Under-Optimized Region Refinement and Progressive Post-Training
summary: PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 enhances document parsing performance through targeted data optimization and progressive post-training techniques, achieving state-of-the-art results on OmniDocBench v1.6.

title: MOSS-Image Technical Report
summary: MOSS-Image is an open diffusion transformer that combines high-fidelity synthesis with intent-aware prompt enhancement to generate text-rich, layout-coherent images, achieving state-of-the-art open-weight results on long-form text and layout benchmarks.

title: nanoMuse: An Open-Source Personal Agent for Every Device You Own
summary: Assistants from 2011 answered and waited, and agents from 2023 did a task and stopped. In September 2026 Meta's Muse showed an agent for one person, with accounts, devices, memory and a conversation that lasts, closed, in a vendor's cloud, in one country. Such an agent is expected to act on a person's accounts and devices, remember them across weeks, speak first when it is worth it, and answer for what it did. It is a kind of software, not a model, and until now had no open counterpart. This report defines the personal agent in five questions and three horizons. It reads how Muse is built from Meta's public record and a copy of its production prompt, each statement marked by its source. It then presents nanoMuse, the open-source counterpart under the GPL-3.0, one agent on every device a person owns, with hands on the phone's screen and the computer's. They share one conversation over a relay anyone can run; every action goes through a Sentinel, memory is files the person can read, and the model is their choice. Its size and cost are given as estimates. What is open, memory with provenance, an evaluation suite for the hands and an open model for them, is set out as a roadmap.

title: SpecPilot: Autonomous Algorithm Discovery and Systems Optimization for Speculative Decoding
summary: SpecPilot autonomously discovers deployment-specific algorithms and system optimizations to maximize speculative decoding speedups across diverse models, drafters, and serving regimes without quality loss.

title: OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching
summary: OmniEdu is a family of instruction-tuned educational foundation models that improve K-12 problem solving, curriculum understanding, and tutoring through capability-balanced training data.

title: Xiaomi-OCR-0 Technical Report
summary: Xiaomi-OCR-0 is a compact vision-language model that unifies document parsing and OCR understanding through automated data synthesis, progressive training with text anchoring and reinforcement learning, and achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks.

title: Differentiable Data Augmentation with Kornia
summary: This paper reviews the Kornia differentiable data augmentation module for both 2D and 3D tensors, integrating with PyTorch's autograd and optim, and benchmarks it against other frameworks.

title: A decoder-only foundation model for time-series forecasting
summary: A large language model adapted for time-series forecasting achieves near-optimal zero-shot performance on diverse datasets across different time scales and granularities.

title: TailSteer: Trajectory-Tail Steering for Drift-Resistant Multi-turn Image Editing
summary: TailSteer, a final-stage training framework, reduces cumulative visual drift in multi-turn editing by keeping early denoising dynamics close to the base model and learning tail-focused preservation corrections from on-policy rollouts, preserving pretrained generative and editing abilities.

Its intuitive interface combines AI workflow, RAG pipeline, agent capabilities, model management, observability features (including [Opik](https://www.comet.com/docs/opik/integrations/dify), [Langfuse](https://docs.langfuse.com), and [Arize Phoenix](https://docs.arize.com/phoenix)) and more, letting you quickly go from prototype to production. Here's a list of the core features: ## Quick start > Before installing Dify, make sure your machine meets the following minimum system requirements: > > - CPU >= 2 Core > - RAM >= 4 GiB The easiest way to start the Dify server is through [Docker Compose](docker/docker-compose.yaml). Install [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) with a running daemon, Docker Compose v2.35.0 or later, and OpenSSL. For a new deployment, run the following commands from the repository root. For an existing deployment, preserve your `.env` and follow the [upgrade guidance](docker/README.md#review-configuration-after-an-upgrade). ```bash cd docker cp .env.example .env openssl rand -hex 32 ``` Open `.env` and set `DIFY_AGENT_LOCAL_SANDBOX_AUTH_TOKEN` to the generated value. Keep the default `COMPOSE_PROFILES` value for the bundled services. Service defaults load automatically; no additional configuration files are required. From the same `docker` directory, start the services: ```bash docker compose up -d docker compose ps --all ``` Once the services are running, open [http://localhost/install](http://localhost/install) to complete the initial setup. metadata.readme_excerpt: Paritok A non-destructive compression gateway for coding agents — cut your input-token bill without changing your agent. Paritok sits between your agent and the LLM as a drop-in proxy. On every request it strips the tool-schema bloat, compresses tool results and file reads, and summarizes stale history — then forwards upstream, billed on the compressed tokens. Nothing is ever permanently discarded: the agent pulls back any exact original on demand. Works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, OpenHands , and any agent that honors BASE_URL — you don't change a line of your agent . Powered by the first open-source 4B compression model trained specifically for coding agents (45K real agent trajectories). Cut input token bills from ~25% on turn one to past 85% in long, context-saturated sessions , and fit ~3× more turns in the same context window. metadata.readme_excerpt: ![Caveman Compression](images/banner.png) **Lossless semantic compression for LLM contexts** [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-blue.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT) [![Python 3.8+](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.8+-blue.svg)](https://www.python.org/downloads/) [Quick Start](#quick-start) • [Examples](#examples) • [Benchmarks](#benchmarks) • [Spec](SPEC.md) --- ## What is this? Strip grammar. Keep facts. Save tokens. ```diff - "In order to optimize the database query performance, we should consider implementing an index on the frequently accessed columns..." (70 tokens) + "Need fast queries. Check which columns used most. Add index to those columns..." (50 tokens) = 29% reduction ``` --- ## How It Works ![How Caveman Compression Works](images/info.png) LLMs excel at filling linguistic gaps. They predict missing grammar, connectives, and structure. **Key insight:** We remove only what LLMs can reliably reconstruct. **What we remove (predictable):** - Grammar: "a", "the", "is", "are" - Connectives: "therefore", "however", "because" - Passive constructions: "is calculated by" - Filler words: "very", "quite", "essentially" **What we keep (unpredictable):** - Facts: numbers, names, dates - Technical terms: "O(log n)", "binary search" - Constraints: "medium-large", "frequently accessed" - Specifics: "Stockholm", "99.9% uptime" ``` Compressed: "Company medium-large. Location Stockholm." Decompressed: "at a medium-large company based in Stockholm" ↑ grammar added, facts unchanged ↑ ``` --- ## Quick Start ### Installation **LLM-based (best compression, requires OpenAI API):** ```bash python3 -m venv venv source venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt # Set up API key cp .env.example .env # Edit .env and add your OpenAI API key ``

Results are verified source with exact line ranges: treat them as already read. Use Grep only to confirm an exact literal in a file you already know, or to count. For questions asking for every/all sites, run one repo_search per distinct pattern (queries=[...]) and follow the refs. If the tools are listed as deferred, load them with ToolSearch first. | Need | Tool | |---|---| | Find code by behavior, concept, error text or identifier | `repo_search` (`queries=[...]` for several at once; `under`, `language`, `path_glob` to narrow) | | Explain how/why across several files, with citations | `context_answer` | | Definition, callers, callees, importers, references of a symbol | `symbol_graph` (several names: `A\|B\|C`) | | Multi-hop impact before a change | `graph_query` | | Code that may live in another indexed repo | `cross_repo_search` | Before editing, fetch every involved symbol in one call; before a rename or signature change, get every site with `symbol_graph` `query_type=references`. metadata.readme_excerpt: # RedKnot + DeepInfer The DeepInfer-based development track of **RedKnot**, an open-source project for efficient long-context LLM serving. [Website](https://rednote-machine-learning.github.io/RedKnot/) · [RedKnot paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06256) · [Upstream DeepInfer](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer) · [Apache-2.0 license](LICENSE) **Status:** This branch starts from the complete [DeepInfer baseline at `5537415`](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer/commit/553741557a57df44a46fb3ab72b6aafeaf945337), including its pinned submodules. metadata.readme_excerpt: Long-term memory for AI assistants — fast, private, and yours. # AutoMem [AutoMem](https://automem.ai) gives your AI a memory that survives the chat. Save the decisions, preferences, notes, and context that matter. The next time you open Claude, Cursor, Codex, ChatGPT, or another connected assistant, it can bring back the right details instead of making you repeat yourself. Ask, "Why did we choose PostgreSQL?" and AutoMem can return the decision, the alternatives you considered, the principle behind it, and the work that followed — not just a pile of similarly worded snippets. ## Why AutoMem feels different **No LLM call in the middle of recall.** AutoMem looks up memories directly through its graph and vector index. That keeps normal retrieval fast and avoids an extra generative-LLM charge every time your assistant needs context. It still uses embeddings — from Voyage, OpenAI, or a local provider — and optional enrichment can add more structure over time. **More than vector search.** A vector match finds something similar; AutoMem also records typed relationships between memories. It can follow the connections between a decision, its rationale, and its consequences, so your assistant has a better chance of returning the *why*, not only the words it recognizes. **One memory across your tools.** Use the local MCP bridge with Claude Desktop, Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, and more. For cloud agents, Remote MCP connects the same service to ChatGPT Developer Mode, Claude.ai, and ElevenLabs over HTTPS. Your memory is not locked to one chat app. **Own the data and the setup.** Run AutoMem locally with Docker, on your own infrastructure, or as a small Railway service group. It exposes both MCP and a REST API, so it fits into the tools and workflows you already use. ## Pr

While various model-based methods have improved sample efficiency by learning interactive world models, these agents tend to be "short-sighted", as they are typically trained on short snippets of imagined experiences. We argue that the primary challenge in open-world decision-making is improving the exploration efficiency across a vast state space, especially for tasks that demand consideration of long-horizon payoffs. In this paper, we present LS-Imgine, which extends the imagination horizon within a limited number of state transition steps, enabling the agent to explore behaviors that potentially lead to promising long-term feedback. The foundation of our approach is to build a long short-term world model . How can reinforcement learning agent successfully learn with such raw data, where signals can be strongly entangled with noises? Denoised MDP characterizes information into four distinct types, based on controllability and relation with rewards, and proposes to extract a state representation space containing only information both **controllable** and **reward-relevant**. Under this view, several prior works can be seen as insufficiently removing noisy information. To properly extract *only* the useful signal, Denoised MDP considers novel factorized MDP transition structures, where **signal** representation and **noise** representation are separated into distinct latent spaces. The state abstraction (i.e., representation learning) problem is turned into a regularized model fitting problem: fitting the factorized forward model to collected trajectories, while requiring the **signal** latents to be minimally informative of the raw observations. While many recent works have taken essential steps on GAN-generated faces, more threatening attacks related to identity swapping or diffusion models are still overlooked. And the forgery traces hidden in unknown attacks from the open-world unlabeled faces remain under-explored. To push the related frontier research, we introduce a novel task named Open-World DeepFake Attribution, and the corresponding benchmark OW-DFA and OW-DFA++, which aims to evaluate attribution performance against various types of fake faces in open-world scenarios. ## Dataset - Prepare Deepfake Detection datasets | Dataset | Paper | Link | | :-------------: | :-------------------------------------------------------------------: | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------: | | FaceForensics++ | FaceForensics++: Learning to Detect Manipulated Facial Images | [Paper](https:

title: Scaling Up Analog CIM: A Simulation Framework for Topology-Aware Mapping
summary: Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) enables energy-efficient AI inference by performing in-situ matrix multiplication. The growing demand for deploying larger models motivates chiplet integration to expand CIM capacity. However, simulation abstractions based on local operator costs and aggregate communication metrics obscure the impact of weight-mapping topology when CIM system scales up. We develop a phase analysis that quantifies how strongly mapping topology affects system performance across hardware configurations and how mapping optimization translates into latency gains. To evaluate and exploit this design space, we present Isobar, a simulation platform integrating CIM decompositions, heterogeneous execution, and resource modeling. Validated against silicon measurements and cycle-accurate simulation, Isobar provides reliable cost estimates that enable effective mapping search across model and hardware configurations. For Gemma-7B prefill, Isobar-guided mapping reduces communication time by 23.3% and end-to-end latency by 18.6% relative to the strongest baseline. Isobar's system-level modeling show that analog CIM retains energy-efficiency potential relative to GPU when scaled to thousands of dies, and identify topology-aware mapping as a key design dimension for efficient execution.

title: When Less is More: Emerging Network-Wide Use Cases for Hollow-Core Fibers in Optical Networks [Invited]
summary: Hollow-Core Fiber (HCF) is emerging as a disruptive technology for next-generation optical networks, offering 30\% lower propagation latency than standard Single-Mode Fiber (SMF), record-low attenuation (0.05-0.1 dB/km), and nonlinearities reduced by three to four orders of magnitude. While the physical-layer benefits of HCF have been extensively demonstrated, recent industrial commitments by hyperscalers (e.g., Microsoft, Amazon) and the rapid maturation of nested antiresonant nodeless fibers (NANF) call for a systematic assessment of the impact of HCF at the network level. Building on a series of prior contributions, we overview four emerging network-wide use cases for the selective deployment of HCF in hybrid SMF/HCF networks: (i) latency-constrained Edge Data Center (edgeDC) consolidation; (ii) energy-efficient high-power amplification; (iii) capacity scaling via single-fiber bidirectional (BiDi) transmission; and (iv) coexistence of classical and quantum (QKD) channels. Consolidated results across realistic metro, national, and continental topologies convey a unifying message: in each use case, a selective HCF upgrade captures a significant share of the achievable benefit compared to a network overhaul. The required HCF budget is use-case-specific, i.e., 6-24\% of the total network fiber length for edgeDC consolidation (up to 50\% fewer edgeDCs), 40\% of the network links for QKD/classical coexistence (up to 38\% fewer quantum modules), and 40-60\% of the network links for energy-efficient capacity scaling via BiDi-HCF (up to 28\% lower network power per Tbps and 70\% more served traffic, at half the HCF strand count of a unidirectional HCF upgrade), whereas for energy-efficient high-power amplification the gain keeps growing with the HCF budget (up to 60\% lower network power per Tbps at the national scale) and what saturates is the benefit of increasing the EDFA output power.

title: SensorGuard-RV: Sensor-to-Register Data Protection for Resource-Constrained RISC-V Devices
summary: Embedded systems rely on sensor measurements that traverse a complex hardware-firmware stack (e.g. peripheral interfaces, communication buses, memory, and drivers) before reaching the applications that use them. At worst, an attacker with access to this path may successfully intercept, overwrite, fabricate, or replay readings. This may cause systems that act on such data, such as flight controllers and industrial processes, to behave incorrectly or unsafely. Existing defences, such as trusted execution environments and trusted I/O paths, still depend on trusted driver software and correctly configured access control, which remain fragile in practice. In response, we present SensorGuard-RV, a hardware-first approach that delivers sensor samples into processor registers without trusting intermediate software, buses, or memory. After configuration, a write-once ownership switch hands the sensor to a fixed-function controller that performs hardware-level authenticated encryption on sensor samples under a key inaccessible to software. We develop a new RISC-V instruction then instructs the CPU to decrypt the sample and writes it to a register only after verifying its tag and rejecting replays, including across resets. We implement SensorGuard-RV on the NEORV32 core with an ADXL362 SPI accelerometer on an Artix-7 FPGA. At 100 MHz, a protected sample reaches a register in 5,191 cycles (51.9 $μ$s), of which the two Ascon authenticated encryption engines account for 30. Because fixed-function acquisition removes per-byte software polling, the protected loop sustains 19,015 transactions/s, 5.3% above a software-driven SPI baseline. The added logic (3,155 LUTs and 2,215 registers; 5.0% and 1.7% of the device) is dominated by the Ascon engine and preserves the 100 MHz clock, while estimated power rises from 118 to 368 mW.

title: StrataFlux: Memory-Hierarchy-Native Low-Bit LLM Inference
summary: Quantization reduces the memory and bandwidth demands of large language model (LLM) inference but can degrade accuracy; offloading higher-precision data can instead stall generation. We introduce StrataFlux, a framework that challenges this tradeoff by recovering accuracy lost to low-bit weight and key-value (KV) cache quantization while retaining quantization's memory and speed advantages. StrataFlux co-designs refinement representation, selection, and delivery to make host RAM and solid-state drives useful sources of additional precision. Its selective precision streaming reduces transfer volume, overlaps delivery with computation, and reuses fetched precision across decoding steps so generation need not wait for every transfer. We evaluate 2-4-bit weights and 2-3-bit KV-cache on dedicated GPUs and unified-memory platforms. For 2-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct weights, StrataFlux reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 9.46 to 8.40 while maintaining 95.4% of the quantized base's throughput on RTX 5090. With 2-bit weights and KV, StrataFlux raises Qwen3-8B's AIME 2024/2025 accuracy from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory use. At 128K context, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with 3-bit weights and 2-bit KV achieves comparable perplexity and speed to vLLM's 4-bit AWQ weights and 8-bit KV on RTX 5090, using approximately half the GPU memory. These results show that GPU-resident precision need not set the accuracy ceiling, nor offloading-tier latency dictate decoding speed.

title: Measured Coupling for Parallel Decoding in Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion language models can write many tokens per step, but must choose which tokens are safe to commit together. Mean-field decoding penalizes pairs of positions whose predictions look alike. We replace this proxy with the coupling itself: how much committing one token changes the model's confidence at another. Cheap probes inside the main forward pass measure it, with no training or extra model, and it plugs into the same mean-field rule. On three models and four benchmarks, our method needs far fewer steps than mean-field decoding and is faster in most settings, also with a key-value cache, at an average accuracy cost of 1.1 points. Shuffling the couplings or replacing them with a uniform bonus loses this gain.

title: GINGER: Spicing Up Graph-Based Vector Search
summary: We present \textsc{Ginger}, a state-of-the-art open-source C++ library for graph-based approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS). We developed \textsc{Ginger} at Google to push the speed and memory efficiency of graph search on large and high-dimensional embedding datasets. \textsc{Ginger} surpasses existing ANNS libraries with regards to query throughput and indexing time while matching the memory footprint of the most space-efficient competitors. \textsc{Ginger} builds upon recent advances in proximity graph construction (PiPNN) and vector quantization (TurboQuant). We introduce Nested TurboQuant (NTQ), a two-level quantizer which supports low precision graph navigation and high precision reranking in a single code. This representation achieves near floating point precision with $2.6\times$ less memory. We also compress the size of our proximity graphs by up to $2.5\times$ without impacting query throughput. We combine graph reordering with a new lossless compression codec called AdaptiveGap, which builds upon StreamVByte. At $95\%$ recall, \textsc{Ginger} speeds up query throughput by an average of $1.8\times$ over each dataset's fastest competitor and by at least $2.3\times$ over any single library. This lead grows to $2.9\times$ over compact libraries on high-dimensional embeddings.

title: Should You Split Decode? Disaggregation Across Future Models and Accelerators
summary: For large language model (LLM) inference, prefill/decode disaggregation (P/D) is deployed in production to isolate phases with different resource demands. Attention/feed-forward network disaggregation (AFD) splits decode again, but adds communication, placement constraints, and another provisioned pool. We ask whether role-specific placement repays this cost as models and accelerator roadmaps change. Infrastructure is committed before future models and hardware can be benchmarked. We present SiliconForge, a calibrated model that varies the serving decomposition and hardware assignment independently. We compare P/D and P/D+AFD across four model directions, four accelerator classes anchored to current and announced parts, and two fabrics. We co-optimize each design using the same rules for pipeline overlap and the same power budget. Our main comparisons show no robust deployment-level AFD advantage in service-level objective (SLO) goodput per kW. Most nominal estimates favor P/D. The largest AFD lead comes from fitting one more prefill replica, not from a more efficient decode pool. AFD has a nominal lead in the KV-heavy (key-value) model direction when the co-located expert pool spans several small scale-up domains. Larger domains or a fast fabric for both designs weaken that lead. We therefore find that prefill provisioning, decode memory bandwidth, links, and pool granularity decide deployments more than the split alone. A fixed hardware assignment can lose its advantage as models, fabrics, hardware assumptions, and objectives change. Re-optimizing mappings and pool sizes on the same hardware cuts early commitment's median normalized goodput loss from 36% to 9%. We recommend adjustable mappings and pool sizes to let boundary and hardware choices follow model demands.

title: Beyond Quantum Messages: Toward Quantum-Native Network Functioning
summary: The Quantum Internet is commonly envisioned as a network that transports quantum states and distributes entanglement as the key resource underpinning distributed quantum applications. This view is necessary but incomplete if quantum phenomena are confined to what the network carries or manages, while network functionalities remain grounded predominantly in classical abstractions. This Perspective advances a broader thesis: quantum phenomena can also participate directly in the realization of network functionalities. We first establish the architectural baseline by introducing entanglement as a stateful network resource whose operational condition is non-locally distributed across remote nodes, evolves through manipulation or consumption, and degrades over time through decoherence. Its evolving state must therefore remain visible to the functionalities acting on it. We then move beyond resource visibility and use two mechanisms as proof points of a broader quantum-native functional design space: entanglement generation during propagation through coherent spatial-path superposition, and operational connectivity induced by shared entanglement that can depart from the physical graph. These examples show that paths, neighbors, or participating nodes may become operationally relevant in ways determined by quantum coherence and shared entanglement, rather than by physical connectivity alone. We identify Quantum Addressing as a transversal abstraction capable of representing such relations while complementing, rather than replacing, classical addressing and signaling. The resulting perspective broadens the Quantum Internet from transporting quantum information and distributing entanglement to exploiting quantum phenomena in network functioning, opening a coupled frontier spanning routing, forwarding, control, and functionality placement.

title: Zirah: A Post-Quantum True Random Number Generator Hardware Signer With an Avalanche Noise
summary: Zirah is a hardware signer built around an STM32F407 microcontroller, and its purpose is to find out, on inexpensive hardware, where a post-quantum signing key is exposed and what actually protects it. The device draws every random bit from a reverse-biased 2N3904 junction in avalanche breakdown, amplified by an LM358 and screened by SP 800-90B health tests, computes ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204, hedged) on the STM32 with two-share arithmetic masking of the secret-key multiplications, and adds ECDSA P-256 from an ATECC608 secure element over the same digest, once a person has matched an eight-digit digest prefix on its OLED with the PC and pressed a button. A desktop application and a command-line tool drive the board and verify its output, and because only a 32-byte manifest digest reaches the device, it signs files of any type and size, returning signed copies for PDF, Office Open XML, ZIP, PNG and JPEG files and detached records for every other format. NIST's SP 800-90B tool rejected the IID assumption for 1,000,000 raw samples and assessed 6.898 bits of min-entropy per byte on the non-IID track, against the 1 bit the firmware credits, while spectral lines near 116 Hz that hold about 5 % of the variance remain unexplained. At 168 MHz the masked signature took a median of 157 ms over 20 runs and a complete signing operation under 0.8 s, and the signer matched the pq-crystals reference in 1,976 checks natively and on an emulated Cortex-M4. The ATECC608 can neither store the 4,032-byte ML-DSA-65 key nor compute with it, so that key sits in ordinary flash behind readout protection, and on an earlier board, before that protection was enabled, a debugger copied it out and the copy produced a valid ML-DSA-65 signature without the device, although the leakage results come from an instruction-level emulator and nothing here is certified.

title: AI-Native Task-Oriented Semantic Communications over a Relay: Benefits and Vulnerabilities
summary: Semantic communication (SemCom) using a relay node is considered, where the relay assists in conveying task-relevant information from a source to a destination, with meaning defined by classification labels. A joint end-to-end design of the source encoder, relay transformation, and destination decoders is developed to optimize both semantic inference accuracy and perceptual reconstruction quality for image data. Relay-assisted schemes are shown to outperform direct transmission, with gains that become more pronounced in low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regimes across different relaying strategies. Alongside these performance benefits, however, a key security vulnerability introduced by the relay is identified, and a Byzantine attack is formulated in which the relay injects structured, learned perturbations into its transmitted signal. The attack operates on intermediate communication representations subject to channel effects, with perturbations generated through a learned mapping applied at test time. It is shown to significantly degrade semantic inference accuracy at the destination. These results reveal a clear trade-off between SemCom gains and security risks in relay-assisted systems, motivating the need for secure relay designs that account for insider threats.

title: MCUFlowNet: Hardware-Aware Neural Architecture Search for Optical Flow on Microcontrollers
summary: Dense optical flow allows small drones to avoid obstacles. However, few dense optical flow networks are designed for microcontrollers (MCUs) with neural accelerators, whose on-chip SRAM limits the input resolution. We present PACE-NAS, a macro-to-micro neural architecture search framework that decouples memory from latency: a macro design fixes the backbone and its peak SRAM, and a micro design searches operators and depths to trade accuracy against compiler-estimated latency. We apply it to EdgeFlowNet on a Grove Vision AI V2 board (Ethos-U55), where profiling locates the peak SRAM at the full-resolution output head. Replacing transposed convolutions with bilinear upsampling and convolutions lowers the peak SRAM by 18%, and two lightweight context modules lower the endpoint error (EPE) without raising the peak. All searched subnets share this peak, so the search needs no memory constraint. We name the Pareto-optimal models MCUFlowNet; the fastest variant, MCUFlowNet-S, runs 1.76x faster than a retrained EdgeFlowNet at a 1.6% higher EPE and, in simulated forest flights at 2 m/s, reaches the goal without collision in 51.5% of trials, against 41.8%. PACE-NAS also applies to semantic segmentation, where a searched PIDNet-S variant runs 1.17x faster at similar accuracy. Code is available at https://gitlab.kuleuven.be/emedia-research-lab/esat-stadius/mcuflownet/mcuflownet.

title: Post-Quantum Authentication of IoT Data on Ethereum: Signatures, the Calldata Floor, and Device-Signed Merkle Roots
summary: Field devices deployed today will still be producing records when quantum computers may break their signatures, so systems that anchor IoT data on blockchains need a post-quantum (PQ) authentication path now. We measure its cost on Ethereum under the current execution rules, including the EIP-7623 calldata floor and the EIP-7825 transaction cap, and under the calldata repricing scheduled for the Glamsterdam upgrade. We combine device-side measurements of ML-DSA, Falcon, SLH-DSA, LMS and XMSS, reproduced costs of open-source Solidity verifiers, a new standard-compliant LMS/HSS verifier for SHA-256 and SHA-256/192, and complete transactions on an Osaka-rule EVM, priced with today's verifiers and with proposed precompiles. Three results stand out. Signing every record costs 8.7 times as much as ECDSA even with an ML-DSA precompile, because the calldata floor rather than verification sets the price. When each device signs a Merkle root over 100 records, a standard LMS verifier available today costs about 3,350 gas per record, against 245 gas for ECDSA in the same design, and it is unaffected by the scheduled repricing, which raises floor-bound designs by up to 1.9 times. With the proposed precompiles, ML-DSA-44 costs 1,031 gas per record, and a hybrid ECDSA and ML-DSA signature adds only 2.5%. Post-quantum device authentication is therefore deployable on Ethereum without protocol changes, provided that the latency of batching and the data-availability properties of the chosen variant fit the application.

title: GUARDTs: Decentralized Access Control for Replicated Data Types
summary: Replicated data types providing strong eventual consistency offer a principled foundation for developing decentralized software. Yet existing approaches to programming such data types leave access control unresolved: they either provide none at all, delegate it to a trusted coordinator, reintroducing the centralization they were designed to avoid, or tie it to specific data-type constructions, while typically assuming non-Byzantine replicas and static policies. We present GUARDTs: Guarded Unforgeable Algebraic Replicated Data Types, which embed fine-grained permissions directly into the application data model, operate without a central authority, support dynamic policy evolution, and tolerate Byzantine replicas. We formally prove that GUARDTs guarantee confidentiality, integrity, and availability and show empirically that their access control adds negligible overhead on top of the cost of Byzantine-resilient replication itself.

title: Quantum Advantage in Local Certification of Graph Properties
summary: Local certification allows network vertices to verify global properties using certificates from an untrusted prover and communication with their neighbors. Its complexity is the maximum certificate size at any vertex. Fraigniaud et al. (ITCS 2021) introduced the distributed quantum Merlin-Arthur (dQMA) model and proved an exponential quantum advantage for distributed equality, measured in input-string length. We resolve a question of Hasegawa, Kundu, and Nishimura (PODC 2024) by establishing unconditional exponential and polynomial quantum advantages for graph properties, which depend only on network topology, with complexity measured in the number $n$ of vertices. For every fixed integer $μ\ge 1$, we construct a graph property admitting a one-round dQMA protocol with $O(μ\log n)$-qubit certificates and messages, whereas every $μ$-round distributed Merlin-Arthur (dMA) protocol requires $Ω(n/(μ\log^2 n))$-bit certificates. We also give a one-round dQMA protocol for graph symmetry, the existence of a nontrivial automorphism, with $\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})$-qubit certificates. This yields a polynomial advantage over one-round dMA protocols, for which an $Ω(n^2)$-bit certificate lower bound is known.

title: xDSL-CCPP: An alternative code generator for atmospheric modelling
summary: The Common Community Physics Package (CCPP) is a framework designed to simplify the exchange of physics packages between state-of-the-art atmospheric models. A core software component of CCPP is a code generator: a bespoke Python-based application that uses regular expressions to transform an input specification into Fortran source code. While the code generator initially provided a simple transformation capability, the demands of state-of-the-art atmospheric models have resulted in significant increases in its complexity. Furthermore, ongoing code modernisation efforts to enable GPU-based computing have placed additional demands on the code generator for which it was never designed. Domain Specific Languages (DSLs) have proven to be highly effective in High Performance Computing (HPC), offering the ability to simplify code modernisation efforts. However, traditionally the effort and specialist skills required in the development of a DSL have been a blocker to adoption. In recent years, however, there have been great advances in compiler technologies, and frameworks such as MLIR and xDSL have the potential to greatly lower this barrier to entry. In this paper, we present xDSL-CCPP, a new application-specific code generator based upon the latest MLIR and xDSL compiler technologies, for CCPP. Demonstrating a reduction in bespoke tooling code of around three times, from approximately 15,000 LoC to 5,000 LoC, we highlight the opportunities provided by these compiler frameworks and demonstrate how they significantly lower the barrier to development of HPC application-specific DSLs whilst maintaining application performance and promoting flexibility.

title: Precision - Preserving Subtensor Inference for a 22B Joint Audio - Video Generator under a Fixed GPU Working Set
summary: Complete-block offloading reduces model residency but requires each transferred block to fit the GPU budget. We present Precision-Preserving Subtensor Inference (PSI), a fixed-arena runtime that combines sub-block weight streaming with separately managed intermediate state for the BF16 LTX-2.5 22B joint audio-video transformer. The contribution is a construction whose managed GPU footprint is determined by reusable pages, live state, and bounded workspace, together with controls that separate resource use, transport correctness, and numerical fidelity. Its partitioned operators preserve the dense real-arithmetic construction under stated assumptions. Across nine matched full-prompt cases on RTX A6000, modified PSI reduces sampled transformer-process peak memory from 8,578 to 360 MiB relative to official MATH, while mean time for the eleven transformer invocations rises from 247.11 to 349.00 s. Its managed arena is 80 MiB. Complete native generation and a complete-block FLASH path both succeed under a fixed 3 GiB available-memory cap. The matched A6000 comparison and separate DGX Spark service suite both achieve 100% success in complete audiovisual decoding. FFN reuse lowers mean block time by 4.0% with unchanged BF16 outputs; a fixed-arithmetic one-token transport control preserves all saved states bitwise. Targeted bias and attention changes improve local and one-token numerical comparisons, while mean endpoint error increases across nine full-prompt cases. The construction enables BF16 audiovisual inference with an explicit transformer-memory budget and makes numerical fidelity a separate, testable property of the implementation.

title: SEER: A Scalable Event-Driven Runtime for Parallel Execution of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Environments
summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is increasingly used in systems where many entities interact in a shared environment. In these workloads, policy inference can be batched on GPUs, but the CPU-side environment path still updates entity states, resolves local interactions, and builds observations inside each $\mathrm{env.step}$. This path can dominate latency in interaction-intensive workloads after policy batching. Existing vectorized environment interfaces and general event-driven runtimes do not directly address the fine-grained cross-entity work inside one bounded MARL step while preserving the step-level semantics expected by learning systems. We present SEER (Scalable Event-Driven Environment Runtime), a runtime for MARL environment execution under an explicit event-locality contract. SEER models each environment step as a bounded stream of timestamped events. If direct state updates are entity-local and cross-entity effects are represented as ordered future events, SEER can run independent events in parallel while preserving serial-equivalent boundary outputs. To make this contract practical, SEER uses a CAS-based dual-layer event queue: local event queues preserve per-entity causal order, while a parallel executive list exposes ready work to global worker threads. SEER further uses STPA, a preflight-guided thread-pool selection mechanism that combines short runtime traces with static workload and hardware features. We evaluate SEER on two parameterized MARL workloads: compute-intensive UAV swarm control (Aircraft) and communication-intensive wireless management (PCS). On Aircraft, SEER reduces inference latency by 16.2\% over the baseline. On PCS, SEER reduces environment-execution latency by 46.9\%, 19.5\%, and 64.9\% over ROSS-T, NBSE, and ROOT-Sim, respectively.

title: How Far Can Lightweight LLMs Go in Intent-to-SLO Translation?
summary: Intent-based networking (IBN) promises QoS provisioning in which the network derives the configuration from operator-stated goals. Its first step, translating a natural-language intent into enforceable service-level objectives (SLOs) grounded in a live snapshot of the network state, increasingly relies on large language models (LLMs). These large models add cost and energy to the management loop and typically require multi-GPU, cloud-hosted infrastructure. Can lightweight open LLMs take over this step dependably? We answer this question with a five-dimensional evaluation of ten LLMs with <10B parameters from five families, under four prompting setups, on 716 placement intents. We evaluate translation performance, intent validation, hallucination, energy impact, and robustness to diverse phrasing. The best configurations translate intents with a strict F1 of 0.943 and reject up to 191 of 195 invalid intents. With few-shot reasoning, the strongest models hallucinate unsupported QoS requirements in only about one response in a hundred, whereas the zero-shot setup struggles. A translated intent costs 0.044-0.148 Wh of GPU energy without reasoning, and added energy cost for reasoning pays off for the weaker models. Furthermore, we show that realistic rephrasing lowers the rejection of invalid intents in 15 of 16 configurations for the best-performing models, leaving robust intent validation as a key open challenge for reliable IBN. Our code and data are available: https://github.com/ggck43/intent2slo.

title: ZeroRAG: Adaptive Semantic Peer Routing for Decentralized Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a standard approach to enhance the reliability of large language model (LLM) outputs by retrieving documents relevant to a query and supplying them in the LLM prompt. Today's RAG systems collect, index, and serve these documents from centralized stores. In practice, however, documents are owned by organizations, devices, and individuals who cannot or will not surrender custody of them to a central party, e.g., because of privacy, copyright or regulatory compliance. Existing modern decentralized retrieval techniques either reintroduce a coordinating authority, or rely on a global data structure that requires continuous network-wide coordination (e.g., DHTs). We present ZeroRAG, a decentralized routing layer for document retrieval in RAG that performs semantic query routing across an overlay of peers with- out global data structures or centralized orchestration. Documents remain with the peers that own them, and each peer keeps only lightweight local state: a bounded set of neighbor advertisements and a cache of recently routed queries. Using these, ZeroRAG steers each query through a best-first walk that progressively rewires the overlay toward semantically relevant neighbors, so recall improves over time as the network self-organizes. We evaluate ZeroRAG using three real-world workloads and two decentralized baselines. We find that ZeroRAG outperforms baselines in terms of recall and required network messages, approaches the recall and LLM answer accuracy of a centralized document store, self-heals after catastrophic peer failures, and scales to 100 000 peers.

title: Modular Parameterized Model Checking of Threshold-Based Distributed Algorithms
summary: We present a novel approach for model checking fault-tolerant distributed algorithms: instead of building large, monolithic algorithm models, we propose a modular approach where the user decomposes the algorithm into modules, verifies them individually, and replaces them with a synchronous abstraction. To enable our technique, we introduce a new system model that combines aspects of threshold automata and global synchronization protocols. We investigate the expressiveness of our new model, and present a (bounded) model checking procedure as well as a method for checking the correctness of the abstraction step. We implemented the technique and report on promising experimental results on a case study

title: Instantiating the Knowledge Plane
summary: In 2003, Clark et al. proposed the "Knowledge Plane", a layer of intelligent agents that share rich information about network state in order to collaboratively manage the Internet across administrative boundaries. The technology of the day lacked the two capabilities it demanded most: reasoning and unstructured communication. Thus, automated network management has remained largely confined to single domains, while interdomain problems are still resolved by human operators on the phone. We argue that agentic large language models can finally unlock the potential of the Knowledge Plane, but that doing so will require solving new research problems that arise particularly in this decentralized, multi-agent, coopetitive setting that have received limited attention in the literature thus far.

title: CAMP: Context-Aware Mapping and Placement for LLMs on 3D-IMC Arrays
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) incur severe memory-access overheads due to the cost of loading large weight matrices and key-value (KV) caches. Analog In-Memory Computing (AIMC) is an emerging solution that enables computation directly on static weights stored in memory, substantially reducing energy and latency. 3D-IMC further stacks memory arrays into vertical tiers, increasing capacity but revealing a new challenge: how weights are placed in memory determines which matrix-vector multiplications (MVMs) can execute concurrently, affecting latency and throughput. The concurrency aspect of 3D-IMC weight-mapping remains underexplored in the literature, leading to sub-optimal utilization of compute resources on 3D-IMC chips. In this context we propose CAMP (Context-Aware Mapping and Placement), an inference-context-aware weight mapping algorithm for 3D-IMC-based LLM accelerators. CAMP captures the potential resource contention resulting from the architecture, targeted network, and runtime context in a conflict matrix, enabling throughput-optimized weight mapping. This mapping is refined through a profiling-driven feedback loop that efficiently prunes the search space and returns optimized mappings within practical runtimes. CAMP is an offline, software-based solution requiring no hardware changes and improving 3D-IMC compute utilization from 42.4% to 60.3%, delivering up to 2.0x higher 3D-IMC throughput and 1.74x higher end-to-end throughput over state-of-the-art mapping algorithms.

title: OpenRDMA: A GPU-Native Multi-Path Reliable RDMA Transport Architecture
summary: As the computing power density of large-scale AI clusters rises, network communication increasingly limits system performance. GPU-initiated communication requires low-overhead request submission to overlap communication with computation. However, GPUDirect RDMA (GDR) still relies on CPU involvement in its control path, while InfiniBand GPUDirect Async (IBGDA) requires GPUs to assemble Work Queue Entries (WQEs), consuming additional SM resources and memory bandwidth. We propose OpenRDMA, an open-source multi-path reliable RDMA transport architecture designed for GPU-friendly communication. First, OpenRDMA provides a minimal GPU doorbell mechanism: the GPU issues an 8-byte token, and a dedicated FPGA NIC reconstructs the complete WQE from preconfigured context. Second, building on Multipath Reliable Connection (MRC), OpenRDMA supports per-packet multi-path transport and out-of-order arrivals, while selective retransmission, ordered DMA placement, and GPU-visible flag polling provide reliable delivery and safe data consumption. Third, a hardware-software co-designed retransmission mechanism keeps the GPU submission path lightweight and reduces FPGA hardware state overhead: the NIC handles fast data transfer, while CPU software manages complex timeout detection, state tracking, and recovery policies. We describe the architecture and key hardware components of OpenRDMA; implementation of the FPGA prototype is underway.

title: SEROA: Stable Encrypted-Traffic Representation and Online Adaptation for Service-Aware Networks
summary: Mobile networks are evolving toward service-aware operation to support heterogeneous applications with diverse quality-ofservice (QoS) and quality-of-experience (QoE) requirements. In practice, however, the widespread use of encryption makes service types difficult to observe directly, which limits the deployment of service-aware optimization in operational networks. Recent raw-byte representation learning methods have improved offline encrypted-traffic classification, but their robustness in realistic deployment remains limited due to temporal drift and the lack of explicit labels for online adaptation. This paper proposes Stable Encrypted-Traffic Representation and Online Adaptation (SEROA), a deployment-oriented framework for encryptedtraffic classification in service-aware mobile networks. In the offline stage, SEROA exploits protocol structure to learn temporally stable representations by applying masked modeling to stable fields, protocolaware transformations and contrastive learning to unstable fields, and time-adversarial learning to suppress time-specific cues. In the online stage, SEROA uses feedback records containing QoE measurements, wireless states, and allocation decisions to update the deployed classifier through contextual-bandit learning. Experiments show that SEROA consistently outperforms representative pretrained baselines under both random and time-based evaluation protocols, and remains effective under QoE-driven online adaptation. These results demonstrate the value of stable representation learning and online adaptation for practical service-aware mobile networks.

title: Characterizing CUDA Locality Domains on Blackwell GPUs
summary: Low latency is critical to user experience. As NVIDIA Blackwell and Rubin GPUs advance multi-die scaling, data placement and cross-die communication become increasingly important. However, the latency implications and underlying costs of cross-die communication and die-aware execution remain largely unexplored. In this report, we present a comprehensive evaluation of the Locality Domain (LD) feature introduced in CUDA 13.4. Conducted on a single node equipped with eight NVIDIA B300 GPUs, our study examines three aspects: memory management and access, computation, and communication, to identify the sources of latency and, more importantly, explore how LD can mitigate them. Our measurements show that the benefits of LD depend on data access patterns. Through die-aware adaptations and integration with widely used libraries and tools, we achieve speedups of up to 43.5% for NCCL 2.32.3 (AllGather), 111.3% for nvbandwidth (DtoD), and 37% for DeepGEMM (EP). We also identify non-negligible LD-related GPU memory allocation overhead when allocation sizes exceed 32 MB due to barrier and TLB invalidation, we propose a fix to the GPU driver kernel module (submitted to NVIDIA) and show that overhead could be reduced 7x ~ 10x without requiring any user-code changes.

title: Memory Fit: Architectural Support for Page Placement by Learning Models of Good Behavior
summary: Server main memory is increasingly heterogeneous, incorporating technologies such as zswap, CXL memory expanders, and emerging phase-change memories (PCM). To decide where to place pages, operating systems have to choose between efficient but coarse-grained access bits, out-of-band profiling, or costly runtime instrumentation. This paper proposes memory fit, a hardware abstraction that provides precise and accurate page placement information to an operating system. Memory fit measures how well a page "fits" each type of memory in the system. Memory fit separates the mechanism of measuring affinity between pages and memories from the OS policy of choosing which pages to move when. The paper describes soft trace matching (STM), a computationally and space efficient algorithm to compute memory fit. The key technical insight behind STM is that it can estimate memory fit by comparing accesses to a page with a learned model of "good" traces for a memory. We have implemented memory fit and STM in a BOOMv3 RISC-V processor running Linux 6.6. On extended GUPS, memory fit placements recover 2.2-3.8 times as much of the performance gap to optimal placement as Linux TPP. For Redis with equal DRAM and PCM capacities, placements selected by memory fit recover 80% of the performance gap, versus 19% for TPP, in a placement replay. Memory fit requires only 64 bits of state per 4 KiB page and can be updated on every main-memory access with only a 1.2% overhead of OS kernel notification processing.

title: ZYFA: Speed and Accuracy of FP8 FlashAttention on AMD CDNA4
summary: Attention is a core building block of frontier models and often dominates compute-bound prefill at long context. FP8 matrix instructions offer twice the peak throughput of BF16, but they accelerate only matrix multiplication, and the softmax between the two matrix multiplications of attention runs on vector units that FP8 does not accelerate. On the AMD Instinct MI355X, the vendor's AITER kernels reach 39% of peak FP8 matrix throughput at 32K tokens, compared with 49% in BF16. Attention is also more numerically sensitive to quantization than feed-forward layers, and unlike NVIDIA's Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, the MI355X does not track the completion of matrix instructions in hardware, so overlapping the softmax with the matrix multiplications depends on instruction order. We present ZYFA, prefill kernels for the MI355X built on three techniques: (1) computing each FP8 probability directly from its score with a multiply-add and an integer conversion instead of an exponential; (2) a ping-pong schedule in which one group of threads computes its softmax while another executes its matrix multiplications; and (3) scaling each block of probabilities up by a power of two before rounding, and normalizing by the sum of the rounded probabilities. On attention inputs captured from three models and timed at sustained clock speeds, ZYFA achieves 1.16-1.76x the throughput of AITER. On the Gaussian inputs of kernel benchmarks at 32K tokens, it achieves 1.26-1.37x at head dimension 128 and 1.99x for DeepSeek-style multi-head latent attention. The sustained clock of the MI355X depends on operand values, so throughput on random inputs does not reliably predict throughput on real model activations. At head dimension 128, ZYFA's numerical error is within a few percent of that of Composable Kernel and Triton and 62-78% lower than that of AITER's. The source code is available at https://github.com/Zyphra/zyfa.

title: When Does Blockwise Additivity Break? Diagnosing and Repairing the Additive Assumption in Distillation-Based Architecture Search
summary: Blockwise distillation methods for architecture search, such as DNA, DONNA, LANA and Puzzle, score each candidate replacement block in isolation and assemble a child network by minimizing the sum of per-block scores. We test this additive assumption on DeiT-S and DeiT-B with seven replacement blocks per layer, seven block-latency budgets from 70% to 40%, three fine-tuning seeds and paired bootstrap confidence intervals. (i) At mild compression the additive integer linear program (ILP) is close to a pairwise integer quadratic program (IQP) that models block interactions, but the post-fine-tuning gap widens sharply between the 60% and 55% budgets: at 55%-40% the ILP trails the IQP by 3.3-16.6 top-1 points on ImageNet-100. (ii) We split the KL additivity error into a metric component, caused by the non-linearity of the KL in summed logit changes and computable from cached single-block logits, and a functional component, the score-level effect of non-additive logit changes. The metric component accounts for most of the error on DeiT-S (59-65%), the functional component for most of it on DeiT-B (73-76%). (iii) A hybrid search ranks moves with the logit-sum predictor and measures only the best ones. It needs no dedicated pair measurements, costs 13-27% of the IQP's pair stage, and on ImageNet-100 significantly outperforms the IQP in 7 of 14 settings, with no significant difference in 6 and a significant loss in 1. Further reducing the pre-fine-tuning KL, or scoring after a short fine-tune, gives no consistent gain. On full ImageNet-1k with 1000-class fine-tuning, the sharp widening between 60% and 55% (5.8-17.5 points at 55%-40%), the model-dependent decomposition and the hybrid's advantage (significantly better than the IQP in 13 of 14 settings, no the other) are reproduced.

title: KOSMOS: Self-scheduling Persistent Kernels for Communication-Compute Overlap
summary: Tensor and sequence parallelism (TP+SP) and expert parallelism (EP) put collectives on the critical path of transformer layers. State-of-the-art fused kernels mitigate this with fixed roles or schedules, but this rigidity leaves large idle windows. Predicting a communication-computation split does not remove them either; a predetermined split cannot follow data readiness. We present KOSMOS, a library for self-scheduling persistent kernels whose workgroups use queues ordered by consumer demand to switch between communication and computation roles as data become ready, with no scheduler, per-call cost model, or tuned split. KOSMOS fuses every TP+SP collective of a transformer layer with its GEMM, and runs an entire expert layer, from router to fold, in one launch per direction. Evaluated on AMD Instinct MI350X and AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, KOSMOS speeds up TP+SP end-to-end training in Megatron-LM by 1.10-1.28x in BF16 and 1.10-1.25x in MXFP8. KOSMOS accelerates end-to-end training of DeepSeek-V3 and Qwen3-235B proxies by 1.29-1.83x over DeepEP.

title: Understanding Self-Supervised Representation Learning for Encrypted Traffic
summary: SSL has been adopted for encrypted traffic classification to learn representations from unlabeled traces and reduce reliance on manual feature engineering. However, recent studies show that data leakage can inflate reported performance and that pretrained models can underperform shallow classifiers once leakage is controlled. These findings raise questions about what information SSL can learn from encrypted traffic and how different pretraining mechanisms exploit this information. In this paper, we systematically investigate these questions by examining the sources of learnable information, the effectiveness of contextual pretraining, alternative self-supervision mechanisms, and the limits of representation learning. We first find that visible protocol fields retain contextual dependencies that are strongest between adjacent bytes, while payload interventions establish the classification value of retained plaintext structure. Guided by these insights, we investigate byte-level contextual learning through ByteBERT and TrafficDCNet, showing that aligning prediction granularity with local dependencies produces more discriminative representations. We further examine cross-view contrastive learning through AlignTraffic and find that complementary supervision improves representation quality beyond contextual prediction alone. Across four public classification tasks, AlignTraffic outperforms shallow learning by 5.97% to 30.70%, with additional evaluations on industrial traffic demonstrating its effectiveness in broader settings. Finally, evaluations on Tor traffic and individual packets reveal limitations when application information is concealed or unevenly distributed. These findings provide a systematic understanding of how observable information and self-supervision mechanisms shape the effectiveness and scope of representation learning for encrypted traffic.

title: Deep reinforcement learning-based optimization of multi-RAT handovers
summary: A major evolutionary goal and challenge for next-generation wireless systems is seamless multiple radio access technology (multi-RAT) mobility. In a multi-RAT environment, handover decisions must account for both user quality of service and network priorities, including signal quality, resource availability, energy consumption, latency, and security. Although WiFi/cellular mobility is well explored in research and standardization, many conventional handover mechanisms continue to rely primarily on received signal strength. Such decisions may overlook link delay, congestion, and the distinct operating characteristics of heterogeneous RATs. In this work, we present the Reinforced Flexible Multi-RAT Selection framework (ReFlexMRS), a configurable Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL)-based approach for multi-criteria handover target selection. ReFlexMRS is evaluated using an SDN-enabled multi-RAT testbed. The decision problem is formulated as a Markov Decision Process with a finite action space and is addressed using a Deep Q-Network (DQN) with convolutional layers that extract relationships among network measurement features. The agent is trained offline from collected network observations using reward guided Q-value updates, then used to select handover targets during inference. A 5G-WiFi case study demonstrates that ReFlexMRS can trade a small amount of throughput for substantial improvements in link delay, handover stability, and WiFi offloading. Compared with RSSI-based selection, the proposed formulations retain approximately 90-95% of the baseline throughput while reducing total handovers by up to 18% and WiFi-to-5G handovers by up to 13%, while maintaining the required RSSI levels.

title: A Synchronized Tri-Modality Wireless System for Multi-Point Non-Contact Cardiac Monitoring
summary: Cardiac physiological monitoring is fundamental to evaluating cardiovascular health and diagnosing related diseases. Non-contact radar sensing can capture chest-wall vibrations with spatial specificity, enabling localized physiological monitoring and cardiac assessment. Progress, however, has been limited by the absence of a reliable, research-grade hardware platform for rigorous validation of radar-based methods. Prior systems typically pair radar, namely Doppler cardiography (DCG), with only electrocardiography (ECG) or other coarse references, providing no direct mechanical ground truth and thus constraining fine-grained evaluation of radar outputs. We present a tri-modality wireless system that integrates ECG, seismocardiography (SCG), and DCG under a unified acquisition and control framework for time-aligned recording and analysis. The tri-modality system combines miniaturized wearable ECG/SCG modules with a high-resolution mmWave radar module, supporting spatially resolved sensing and subsequent feature extraction. To our knowledge, this is the first integrated ECG--SCG--DCG hardware system for comprehensive cardiac monitoring; it enables multi-point thoracic acquisition, achieves precise cross-modal synchronization, and maintains specifications suitable for wearable operation. Experiments on a linear-motion platform show close agreement between DCG- and SCG-derived displacements, confirming accurate displacement measurement. Human-subject studies further demonstrate cross-modal consistency and robust extraction of feature points, establishing ECG as the electrical anchor and SCG as the mechanical ground truth for DCG. Overall, the system provides a rigorous, spatially resolved validation platform that advances non-contact cardiac sensing and supports next-generation radar-based monitoring.

title: Rule-Guided and Trajectory-Aware Repair for LLM-Based HLS Generation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) offer a promising path for directly generating functionally correct and synthesizable HLS-C from natural-language specifications. However, existing approaches often struggle to turn multi-round tool feedback and reusable HLS knowledge into effective revisions, limiting end-to-end generation success. We propose MementoHLS, an agentic HLS generation framework built around executable and falsifiable dual-memory-guided repair. MementoHLS combines an Executable Repair Contract Library (ERCL), which converts cross-task HLS knowledge into evidence-gated repair actions, with a Reviewer-Grounded Falsification Ledger (RFL), which converts task-local repair history into trajectory evidence to suppress ineffective routes and preserve validated progress. To ensure reliable outcome attribution, a Same-Candidate Reviewer binds Parse, Compile, Testbench (TB), and Synthesis (Synth) outcomes to the corresponding candidate, while a Single-Commit Arbiter commits at most one candidate per round. Evaluated on 94 HLS-Eval and 170 Bench4HLS tasks, MementoHLS improves same-candidate TB$\wedge$Synth pass@1/pass@5 from 41.7%/57.4% to 58.9%/68.1% on HLS-Eval, and from 15.5%/32.9% to 32.4%/50.6% on Bench4HLS, demonstrating substantial improvements in end-to-end HLS generation reliability.

title: Energy Measurement and Optimization of TinyML in Resource-Constrained Embedded Systems: A Systematic Mapping Study
summary: The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has increased the volume of data generated at the network edge, where many devices operate under severe memory, processing, and energy constraints. In this context, Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) enables machine learning (ML) tasks to be executed on microcontrollers, smart sensors, and other resource-constrained platforms. However, the literature remains heterogeneous regarding the algorithms evaluated, energy-measurement methods, reported metrics, influencing factors, and optimization strategies. This study presents a systematic mapping of energy-aware TinyML research. It identifies the main models and learning approaches, classifies energy-evaluation methodologies and metrics, examines the technical factors affecting energy consumption, and organizes the reported optimization techniques into a structured taxonomy. The findings highlight the frequent use of convolutional and lightweight architectures, direct measurements and analytical estimations, and factors related to model architecture, hardware, communication, numerical precision, and input characteristics.
